Mounting the Podman socket gives Traefik the full authority of the Podman API. If Traefik is compromised, an attacker could inspect container metadata and environment variables, start or stop containers, and execute code with the Podman service account’s privileges. A `:ro` mount still allows API write operations. A rootless socket grants the authority of its owning user and covers that user’s containers. A rootful socket grants host-root authority. [Podman API documentation](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-system-service.1.html)

Two safer ways to automate discovery are:

- **Generated Traefik configuration.** A host-side process can watch Podman events and update Traefik’s file provider with the routes it needs. Traefik receives routing configuration without socket access. [Traefik file provider](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/providers/file/)
- **A restricted API proxy.** A separate service holds the socket and forwards only the endpoints Traefik needs for discovery, such as container listing, inspection, and events. This blocks container-management operations through Traefik, though inspection responses can still expose sensitive metadata. [Traefik Docker provider](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/providers/docker/)

I found no Traefik deployment files or Podman installation in the workspace. Socket access is pending your approval. If you accept direct access, please confirm the target Podman account and share the Traefik deployment configuration or its location. I’d configure Traefik to discover containers under that account and publish routes only for containers labeled `traefik.enable=true`.
